title: Accessibility and Assistive Technology
summary: People use websites with keyboards, screen readers, zoom, voice control, and many other tools.

subtopics.title: Semantic structure
subtopics.explanation: Semantic HTML names a page part by its purpose. A button is an action; a link moves somewhere. Screen readers use these built-in roles, and browsers provide keyboard behavior for many native controls. It is like using labeled doors instead of blank panels. Start with the correct element before adding ARIA. In practice, a native button responds to Space and Enter, while a clickable div needs extra keyboard work. In a real page, use a nav landmark for primary navigation so a screen-reader user can jump to it.

subtopics.title: Accessible names
subtopics.explanation: An accessible name tells assistive technology what a control does. A visible label is usually best for an input. Icon-only buttons need a clear name, such as “Close menu.” It is like putting readable text on a switch. Check that the name remains useful when read without nearby visual context. In practice, give a search field a visible label so its purpose remains clear after its placeholder disappears. In a real page, associate an input with a visible label that stays available after typing.

subtopics.title: Keyboard access
subtopics.explanation: Every action should be reachable by keyboard, focus should be visible, and the order should match the task. It is like providing a continuous path through a building. Avoid custom controls that ignore standard keys. Test Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and Escape where they apply. In practice, a modal should move focus into its content and return focus to its trigger when closed. In a real page, when a dialog opens, place focus inside and return it after closing.

subtopics.title: Assistive technology
subtopics.explanation: A screen reader announces page structure, names, and status to someone who cannot see the screen. Zoom and voice control are other tools people may use. It is like hearing a guide describe the building while walking through it. Test real interactions rather than relying only on automated scans. In practice, announce a save result with a status region without moving the person away from the form. In a real page, use a live status message for saved feedback without taking focus away.

subtopics.title: Inclusive feedback
subtopics.explanation: An error should identify the field and explain how to fix it. A status update should be announced when it changes without moving focus unexpectedly. It is like giving directions after a wrong turn. Helpful feedback lets people recover and continue without losing their place. In practice, run a keyboard-only task from the first link through final confirmation before release. In a real page, check a multi-step form with keyboard only and with a screen reader.

foundations.overview: Accessibility means people with different abilities can understand and use a website. Semantic HTML, clear names, keyboard access, and useful feedback help many people, including people using screen readers, zoom, or voice control. Think of it like designing a public building with clear signs and more than one usable route. Automated checks help, but test real tasks with keyboard and assistive technology too.
foundations.whyItMatters: Accessible interaction helps people perceive state, navigate controls, and recover from errors. Native semantics are a foundation; testing real tasks reveals issues automated tools miss.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser exposes semantic roles and names through accessibility APIs to assistive tools.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use native HTML, then test keyboard flow and screen-reader announcements.
foundations.businessImpact: Accessible interfaces reach more users and reduce costly task failures.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Make accessibility part of component design and review, not a final patch.
foundations.performanceImpact: Color contrast, focus visibility, and reduced motion affect day-to-day use.
commonUseCases: Design a form that can be completed without a mouse.
Communicate validation errors and save results to assistive technology.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Native elements often work better; incorrect ARIA can make controls harder to use.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Automated scans prove a page is accessible
commonMisconceptions.reality: Tools find some issues but cannot judge whether a task is understandable.

keyTakeaways: Semantic HTML names a page part by its purpose.
An accessible name tells assistive technology what a control does.
Every action should be reachable by keyboard, focus should be visible, and the order should match the task.
A screen reader announces page structure, names, and status to someone who cannot see the screen.
An error should identify the field and explain how to fix it.
